scenarios.title: Customer Support Resolution Agent
scenarios.setup: You are building a customer support resolution agent with the Claude Agent SDK. It handles returns, billing disputes and account issues, many of which are ambiguous when they arrive. The agent reaches backend systems through custom MCP tools: get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund and escalate_to_human. The business target is at least 80% first-contact resolution, with escalation reserved for cases that genuinely need a person.

questions.prompt: Company policy says refunds above $500 need human approval. The system prompt states this rule in bold, and a test suite of 200 conversations passed. In the first month of production, an audit finds 11 refunds between $520 and $1,400 that process_refund executed without escalation. In each case the customer had described financial hardship. What change best guarantees the policy is followed?

options.text: Move the $500 rule to both the top and the bottom of the system prompt, and add a line stating that hardship never justifies an exception to the limit.
options.rationale: Repetition and placement can lower the failure rate, but the rule is still enforced by the model's judgment. Hardship stories are exactly the pressure that caused the misses.

options.text: Add few-shot examples to the system prompt showing hardship cases above $500 in which the agent declines the refund and calls escalate_to_human.
options.rationale: Examples shape behavior but remain probabilistic. A financial policy that must hold on every call needs enforcement outside the model.

options.text: Add a hook that intercepts process_refund calls, blocks any amount over $500, and returns a message telling the agent to call escalate_to_human.
options.rationale: A tool call interception hook enforces the limit in code on every call and redirects the agent to the escalation workflow. The prompt can no longer be talked around.

options.text: Route each process_refund call through a second Claude instance that reads the conversation and approves or rejects the refund before it runs.
options.rationale: This adds another model call per refund and is still a judgment call by an LLM. A simple numeric threshold is better checked in code.

questions.takeaway: When a business rule must hold every time, enforce it with a hook on the tool call rather than with prompt wording.

questions.prompt: process_refund returns isError: true with the text "Operation failed" for every failure. Logs show the agent retrying refunds that were rejected because the order is outside the 30-day return window, sometimes four times in a row. It also tells customers whose refund hit a payment gateway timeout that their refund is not allowed. What should you change first?

options.text: Return an errorCategory, an isRetryable flag and a short customer-facing explanation in each process_refund error so the agent can tell these cases apart.
options.rationale: The agent cannot choose a recovery path when every failure looks the same. Structured metadata lets it stop retrying policy rejections and retry or explain timeouts correctly.

options.text: Add a system prompt rule that process_refund may be retried at most once per conversation, after which the agent apologizes and offers escalation.
options.rationale: Capping retries hides the wasted calls but the agent still cannot tell a timeout from a policy rejection, so customers keep getting the wrong explanation.

options.text: Add exponential backoff inside the MCP server so process_refund retries internally and reports a failure only after five attempts have run out.
options.rationale: Backoff helps transient errors but retries the 30-day window rejection five more times for nothing, and the final error is just as generic as before.

options.text: Split process_refund into separate tools for orders inside and outside the return window so the agent never calls a refund path that will be rejected.
options.rationale: This adds tools and pushes eligibility logic into tool selection. It does nothing for gateway timeouts, which are the other half of the problem.

questions.takeaway: Structured error responses with a category and a retryable flag let the agent pick the right recovery for each failure type.

questions.prompt: First-contact resolution is 62%. A review of 300 escalated tickets finds two patterns. The agent escalates routine in-policy cases, such as a duplicate charge, whenever the customer writes in an angry tone. It also approves competitor price-match requests on its own, although the written policy only covers price drops on the company's own site. Which two changes address both patterns? Select TWO.

options.text: Score each customer message for sentiment and call escalate_to_human automatically when the negative score stays above a set threshold for two turns.
options.rationale: Tone does not measure case complexity. This would make the first pattern worse by escalating more angry but simple cases.

options.text: Add escalation criteria and examples to the system prompt, stating that requests the policy does not cover, like price matching, go to a human.
options.rationale: Explicit criteria with examples fix the unclear boundary. Policy gaps like competitor price matching are a recognized escalation trigger.

options.text: Ask the agent to rate its confidence from 1 to 10 before acting, and route the case to escalate_to_human whenever its own rating comes in below 7.
options.rationale: Self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated. The agent was already confident when it approved price matches it had no policy basis for.

options.text: Train a classifier on two years of historical tickets to predict which conversations need a human, and run it before the agent sees each request.
options.rationale: This needs labeled data and new infrastructure before the cheaper prompt fix has even been tried.

options.text: Instruct the agent to acknowledge frustration and offer to fix in-policy issues, escalating only if the customer then repeats a request for a person.
options.rationale: This keeps simple angry cases with the agent while still honoring a customer who insists on a human.

questions.takeaway: Escalate on policy gaps and explicit requests for a human, not on sentiment or self-rated confidence.

questions.prompt: Some billing conversations run past 40 turns, so older turns are condensed by progressive summarization. In a sample review, the agent later quoted a refund of "about $80" when the customer was owed $84.37, and lost track of which of three order numbers had already been refunded. What is the most effective fix?

options.text: Raise the token threshold that triggers summarization so the full history stays in context for longer before older turns are condensed.
options.rationale: This delays the loss but does not prevent it. Long conversations still reach the threshold and the figures still get compressed.

options.text: Update the summarization prompt to say that all amounts, dates and order numbers must be preserved exactly as they appear in the original turns.
options.rationale: Summaries compress by design, and an instruction to keep every figure exact will still fail on some turns. The facts need a home outside the summary.

options.text: Before each process_refund call, spawn a subagent that rereads the full raw transcript from storage and confirms the amount and the order number.
options.rationale: This adds a subagent and latency to every refund and only checks one action. The agent still reasons from vague facts the rest of the time.

options.text: Keep amounts, order numbers, dates and statuses in a case facts block that is included in every prompt, outside the summarized history.
options.rationale: Transactional facts held in a persistent block are never summarized, so the agent always has exact figures and refund status.

questions.takeaway: Pull transactional facts into a persistent case facts block instead of trusting them to survive summarization.

questions.prompt: Human agents report that escalated tickets arrive with notes like "Customer has a billing problem, please assist." They cannot see the AI conversation, so they ask the customer to repeat everything, and post-escalation satisfaction has dropped. escalate_to_human currently accepts a single free-text reason field. What change best fixes the handoff?

options.text: Attach the full conversation transcript to every escalated ticket so the human agent can read the complete exchange before replying.
options.rationale: The human now has data but must read a long transcript to find the facts, and nothing states what was found or what should happen next.

options.text: Change the escalate_to_human schema to require customer ID, order ID, issue summary, suspected cause, refund amount and recommended action.
options.rationale: Required structured fields make the agent compile a usable handoff every time, giving a human who never saw the conversation what they need to act.

options.text: Give the human support console access to get_customer and lookup_order so agents can rebuild each case themselves from the backend data.
options.rationale: Humans can look up records but still do not know what the customer said, what was tried, or what the agent concluded.

options.text: Add a system prompt instruction telling the agent to write detailed, well-organized escalation notes covering everything a human would need.
options.rationale: Vague guidance like this gives inconsistent notes. A schema with required fields defines what complete means.

questions.takeaway: Escalation handoffs should be structured summaries with required fields, because the human does not have the transcript.

questions.prompt: The tool descriptions were recently rewritten and now clearly separate lookup_order (order and refund status) from process_refund (issues a new refund). Even so, logs show the agent calling process_refund for messages like "Has my refund for order #4471 gone through yet?" The system prompt includes the line: "When a customer mentions a refund, call process_refund promptly to keep resolution times low." What should you do?

options.text: Rewrite that system prompt line so it no longer ties the word refund to process_refund, and let the tool descriptions guide the choice.
options.rationale: A keyword-sensitive instruction is overriding good descriptions. Removing the false association is the smallest change that fixes selection.

options.text: Add few-shot examples to the system prompt in which questions about the status of an earlier refund are routed to lookup_order instead.
options.rationale: Examples fight the conflicting instruction rather than removing it, and every new phrasing that mentions a refund can still trip the keyword rule.

options.text: Add a hook that blocks process_refund whenever lookup_order shows that a refund for the same order has already been issued or is pending.
options.rationale: This stops duplicate refunds but the agent still picks the wrong tool first and never answers the status question it was asked.

options.text: Merge lookup_order and process_refund into one manage_refund tool that checks for an earlier refund and only issues a new one when none exists.
options.rationale: This mixes a read with a write and hides a side effect behind a status question. The misrouting comes from one prompt line.

questions.takeaway: Check the system prompt for keyword-sensitive instructions that override well-written tool descriptions.

scenarios.title: Code Generation with Claude Code
scenarios.setup: Your engineering team uses Claude Code daily for code generation, refactoring, debugging and documentation. The repository is a TypeScript monorepo with a shared CLAUDE.md, several custom slash commands and a few project skills. Developers work on everything from one-line fixes to multi-week migrations. You own the team's Claude Code configuration and are asked to fix workflow problems as they come up.

questions.prompt: A developer who joined last week says Claude never follows the team's API error-handling conventions for her, while it does for the tech lead. Running /memory on both machines shows that the tech lead's session loads ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, which contains those conventions. The repository's CLAUDE.md does not mention them. What is the right fix?

options.text: Add an onboarding script that copies the tech lead's ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md into each new developer's home directory on day one.
options.rationale: Copies drift as soon as the lead edits his file, and the conventions still live outside version control where nobody reviews them.

options.text: Move the error-handling conventions into the project CLAUDE.md or a .claude/rules/ file, and commit that change to the repository.
options.rationale: Team standards belong in project-level configuration that is shared through version control, so every clone loads them.

options.text: Add the import line @~/.claude/CLAUDE.md to the repository's CLAUDE.md so that every developer's session picks up the conventions.
options.rationale: The path resolves to each developer's own home directory, so the new hire imports her own empty file, not the lead's.

options.text: Create an /api-conventions command in .claude/commands/ that prints the conventions, and ask developers to run it when a session starts.
options.rationale: Commands are on-demand. Conventions that must apply to all API code should load automatically, not depend on someone remembering to run a command.

questions.takeaway: User-level CLAUDE.md applies only to that user, so shared standards must live in project-level configuration.

questions.prompt: The team wants everyone to use the same Jira MCP server in Claude Code. A developer committed a working .mcp.json, but it contains his personal API token in plain text, and security has asked for it to be removed. Other developers still need the server to be available automatically when they clone the repository. What should you do?

options.text: Move the Jira server entry into each developer's ~/.claude.json and delete .mcp.json from the repository so tokens stay on their owners' machines.
options.rationale: User scope is for personal or experimental servers. It removes the secret but also removes the shared, automatic setup the team asked for.

options.text: Add .mcp.json to .gitignore and post a template of the file on the team wiki so each developer can add a token and create the file locally.
options.rationale: This hides the secret by taking the config out of version control, so every developer maintains a hand-made copy that drifts.

options.text: Build a small custom MCP server that wraps the Jira REST API and reads a shared service token from a secrets file bundled with the repository.
options.rationale: A standard integration like Jira is better served by an existing server, and bundling a shared token in the repo recreates the original leak.

options.text: Keep the server in the project .mcp.json, replace the literal token with ${JIRA_API_TOKEN}, and have each developer set that variable locally.
options.rationale: Environment variable expansion in project-scoped .mcp.json keeps the shared config in the repo while each developer supplies their own credential.

questions.takeaway: Share MCP servers through project .mcp.json and keep credentials out of it with environment variable expansion.

questions.prompt: You are replacing a homegrown date library with date-fns. A search shows 47 files import it, and some call sites depend on its unusual timezone handling. In an earlier attempt, output from dozens of Grep and Read calls filled the context window before any plan existed. How should you run the next attempt?

options.text: Use direct execution and migrate each file as soon as Grep finds it, so the discovery output never has to be held in context all at once.
options.rationale: A 47-file migration with timezone edge cases needs a design decision up front. Migrating file by file risks rework when a tricky call site turns up late.

options.text: Paste the list of 47 files and their call sites into CLAUDE.md so the analysis is loaded at startup and Claude does not need to search at all.
options.rationale: This puts one-off migration data into a file loaded in every session for every developer, and it goes stale as soon as the code changes.

options.text: Work in plan mode, hand call-site discovery to the Explore subagent so only a summary comes back, then execute the approved plan directly.
options.rationale: Plan mode suits a multi-file change with design choices, and the Explore subagent keeps verbose discovery out of the main context.

options.text: Open 47 separate sessions in direct execution, one per importing file, so that each session has a small context and cannot run out of room.
options.rationale: Independent sessions cannot make a consistent decision about the timezone behavior, and coordinating 47 of them costs far more than one planned run.

questions.takeaway: Plan large multi-file changes in plan mode and isolate verbose discovery in the Explore subagent.

questions.prompt: The team's /dependency-audit skill in .claude/skills/ walks the whole monorepo and prints thousands of lines. After running it, developers notice Claude losing track of decisions made earlier in the same session. Security also wants the skill limited so that it cannot modify files or run shell commands while it runs. Which two changes meet these needs? Select TWO.

options.text: Add context: fork to the frontmatter so that the skill runs in an isolated sub-agent context and only its final result comes back.
options.rationale: Forking keeps the verbose audit output out of the main conversation, which is what was crowding out earlier decisions.

options.text: Add argument-hint to the frontmatter so developers are prompted for a package name and the audit only scans the part they name.
options.rationale: Narrower scans produce less output, but a full audit still floods the session. The output needs isolation, not just trimming.

options.text: Add a line to the skill body telling Claude it must not edit files or run commands during the audit and should only read and report.
options.rationale: An instruction in the body is guidance the model can drift from. Security asked for a limit on what the skill can do.

options.text: Set allowed-tools in the frontmatter to Read, Grep and Glob so the skill has no access to Edit, Write or Bash while the audit runs.
options.rationale: Restricting allowed-tools limits the skill to read-only inspection while it runs, which meets the security requirement in configuration.

options.text: Move the skill to ~/.claude/skills/ so that its output stays in a personal scope and no longer affects the shared project conversation.
options.rationale: Skill location controls who can use it, not where its output goes. It would also take the skill away from the rest of the team.

questions.takeaway: Use context: fork to isolate verbose skill output and allowed-tools to restrict what a skill can do.

questions.prompt: You ask Claude Code to write normalizePhone(), which converts legacy CRM phone strings to E.164. You have rewritten the prose requirements three times, and each version still handles extensions like "x204" and numbers without a country code differently. What should you do next?

options.text: Give Claude three concrete input and output pairs, including one with an extension and one with no country code.
options.rationale: When prose is read inconsistently, two or three concrete examples pin down the transformation far better than more description.

options.text: Write a fuller prose specification that lists every formatting rule in priority order, with a paragraph on each edge case.
options.rationale: Three prose rewrites have already failed. A longer version of the same approach is still open to interpretation.

options.text: Ask Claude to reread its implementation in the same session, list any inconsistencies it finds, and fix them before you look.
options.rationale: The same session shares the reasoning that produced the inconsistency and has no reference for what correct output is.

options.text: Collect 25 examples covering every phone format in the CRM and paste all of them into the request with the prose requirements.
options.rationale: A few targeted examples are enough to show the ambiguous cases. Dozens add noise and invite matching instead of generalizing.

questions.takeaway: When prose requirements are interpreted inconsistently, give two or three concrete input and output examples.

questions.prompt: A developer spends an afternoon in one Claude Code session mapping how payments flow through a legacy service. Early on, Claude correctly named LedgerWriter and RetryQueue as the key classes. Three hours later its answers contradict those findings and refer to "a typical repository pattern" instead of the classes it found. What should the developer do going forward?

options.text: Add a CLAUDE.md rule stating that answers must cite specific class names from this codebase and must not describe generic patterns.
options.rationale: The model is not choosing to be generic. It has lost the earlier findings in a long context, and a rule cannot bring them back.

options.text: Ask Claude to check each new answer against everything it found earlier in the conversation and flag any contradictions first.
options.rationale: The earlier findings are what has degraded, so checking against them in the same context is unreliable.

options.text: Have Claude record key findings in a scratchpad file as it goes, and refer later questions to that file.
options.rationale: A scratchpad file persists findings outside the degrading context, so later answers can rely on what was actually discovered.

options.text: Restart the investigation in plan mode, which keeps exploration read-only and so stops findings being lost as the session grows.
options.rationale: Plan mode controls whether Claude makes changes. It does not protect findings from context degradation in a long session.

questions.takeaway: Counter context degradation in long exploration sessions by persisting key findings in a scratchpad file.

scenarios.title: Multi-Agent Research System
scenarios.setup: You are building a multi-agent research system with the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates work through the Task tool to four subagents: web search, document analysis, synthesis and report generation. Each subagent has its own AgentDefinition with a system prompt and a restricted tool list. The system researches a topic and produces a comprehensive report with citations.

questions.prompt: Reports often ignore the document analysis results, even though that subagent's output looks correct in the logs. The coordinator invokes the synthesis subagent with the prompt "Synthesize the findings gathered so far into key themes." The synthesis agent's replies contain only general knowledge about the topic. What change fixes this?

options.text: Give the synthesis subagent the web search and document analysis tools so it can gather any findings it needs while it writes.
options.rationale: This duplicates work other agents have already done and invites a synthesis agent to start doing research outside its role.

options.text: Update the synthesis AgentDefinition's system prompt to tell it to review the outputs of earlier subagents before naming themes.
options.rationale: The subagent cannot review what it was never given. Subagents do not inherit the coordinator's history.

options.text: Have the synthesis agent reply NEED_FINDINGS when its input looks thin, and make the coordinator watch for that text and resend.
options.rationale: Parsing free text for a control signal is brittle, and it still relies on a later resend instead of passing the data the first time.

options.text: Pass the complete findings from the search and analysis subagents, with source metadata, directly in the synthesis Task prompt.
options.rationale: Subagents start with isolated context, so the coordinator must pass prior findings explicitly in the prompt it sends.

questions.takeaway: Subagents do not inherit the coordinator's context, so pass prior findings explicitly in the Task prompt.

questions.prompt: For a topic split into four independent subtopics, a research run takes about 11 minutes. Coordinator logs show one Task call per turn: it waits for the first web search subagent to finish before starting the second, and so on. The subtopics do not depend on one another. How should you cut latency?

options.text: Submit the four web search requests through the Message Batches API so they run together, then poll until all are done.
options.rationale: Batches have no latency guarantee and do not support multi-turn tool calling, which a search subagent needs.

options.text: Have the coordinator emit all four Task calls in a single response so the subagents run in parallel.
options.rationale: Multiple Task calls in one coordinator response start the subagents at once, which is the intended way to parallelize independent work.

options.text: Give the coordinator the web search tools so it can run the four searches itself and skip spawning subagents.
options.rationale: This loads search work and verbose results into the coordinator's own context and erodes the separation of roles.

options.text: Combine the four subtopics into one broad Task call so a single search subagent covers all of them in one run.
options.rationale: One agent still works through the subtopics in sequence, and a broad prompt tends to cover some of them thinly.

questions.takeaway: Spawn independent subagents in parallel by emitting multiple Task calls in one coordinator response.

questions.prompt: Several reports state that "no peer-reviewed research exists" on subtopics where reviewers easily find papers. Logs show the document analysis subagent returns {"status": "ok", "documents": []} both when the repository search finds nothing and when the repository API times out. What should the subagent return instead?

options.text: On a timeout, return an error with the failure type, the query tried and any partial results, and keep ok for true empty results.
options.rationale: Separating access failures from valid empty results, with context about what was tried, lets the coordinator decide whether to retry or note a gap.

options.text: Keep returning an empty list in both cases, and have the coordinator retry any empty result three times before accepting it.
options.rationale: This wastes retries on true empty results and still cannot tell the coordinator whether a source was down.

options.text: Raise an exception on any repository timeout so the coordinator stops the run rather than finishing with partial coverage.
options.rationale: One failed source should not end the whole workflow when other results are usable and the gap can be reported.

options.text: Return a "repository unavailable" status on timeout, and tell the synthesis agent not to claim that research is absent.
options.rationale: A bare status hides what was attempted and what partial results exist, and the prompt rule only masks one symptom downstream.

questions.takeaway: Distinguish access failures from valid empty results and propagate structured error context to the coordinator.

questions.prompt: Reviewers flag two problems in recent reports. Many claims have no citation, although the search agent found a source for each one. And where two credible surveys give different adoption rates (34% and 41%), the report states one figure as fact and never mentions the other. Which two changes address these problems? Select TWO.

options.text: After drafting, have the report agent reread its own report and add a citation wherever it decides a claim lacks one.
options.rationale: The source links were lost upstream. Rereading the draft cannot recover mappings the agent never received, and it will guess.

options.text: When figures conflict, have the synthesis agent keep the figure from the more recent survey and drop the older one as outdated.
options.rationale: Newer is not the same as correct, and the two surveys may measure different populations. Silently dropping one still hides the conflict.

options.text: Require subagents to return claim-source mappings with claim, excerpt, URL and publication date, and have synthesis keep them.
options.rationale: Structured claim-source mappings carried through synthesis keep attribution from being lost when findings are compressed.

options.text: Give the report agent the web search tools so it can find a source for any uncited claim after the draft has been written.
options.rationale: This gives a writing agent research tools outside its role, and it may attach a different source than the one the claim came from.

options.text: When credible sources disagree, include both values with their sources and note the conflict rather than choosing one.
options.rationale: Annotating conflicts with attribution keeps the report honest and lets readers see that the figure is contested.

questions.takeaway: Preserve claim-source mappings through synthesis and annotate conflicting figures with their sources instead of picking one.

questions.prompt: The document analysis subagent has two tools: analyze_content ("Analyzes content and returns insights") and analyze_document ("Analyzes a document and returns findings"). analyze_document expects a PDF ID from the document store, and analyze_content expects raw web page text. About a third of calls send web text to analyze_document, which returns parse errors. What is the best first step?

options.text: Add five few-shot examples to the subagent's system prompt showing web text going to analyze_content and PDF IDs to analyze_document.
options.rationale: Examples work around two near-identical descriptions instead of fixing them, and they add tokens to every call.

options.text: Set tool_choice to force analyze_content on every turn, since web text is most of the input, and handle PDFs in a separate request.
options.rationale: Forcing one tool breaks the PDF path and moves routing out of the model into a second pipeline you now have to maintain.

options.text: Rename analyze_content to extract_web_results and rewrite both descriptions to state each tool's inputs, outputs and when to use it.
options.rationale: Tool descriptions drive selection. Clear names and descriptions that state inputs and boundaries remove the overlap at its source.

options.text: Add a PostToolUse hook that catches parse errors from analyze_document and resends the same input to analyze_content automatically.
options.rationale: This patches each failure after it happens, adding a wasted call every time while the confusing descriptions stay in place.

questions.takeaway: Fix misrouting between similar tools by renaming them and writing descriptions that state inputs, outputs and boundaries.

questions.prompt: For broad topics, reports often have thin coverage in one or two areas. The coordinator currently runs search, analysis, synthesis and report exactly once, in a fixed sequence. You want the system to close coverage gaps before the report is written. Which design should you use?

options.text: Have the report agent add a Limitations section listing areas where the evidence was thin, so readers know which parts to treat with care.
options.rationale: Disclosing gaps is useful but does nothing to close them, which is what was asked.

options.text: Have the coordinator check the synthesis for gaps, send targeted queries back to search and analysis, and rerun synthesis until coverage is sufficient.
options.rationale: An iterative refinement loop run by the coordinator finds the gaps and re-delegates with targeted queries before the report is produced.

options.text: Have the synthesis agent end its output with COVERAGE COMPLETE when satisfied, and loop the pipeline until the coordinator sees that phrase.
options.rationale: Loop control based on a phrase in free text is fragile, and nothing tells the search agents which gaps to target on the next pass.

options.text: Run the full search, analysis and synthesis sequence three times for every topic and merge the three syntheses before the report step.
options.rationale: Blind repetition triples cost and mostly repeats the same queries, so the thin areas are likely to stay thin.

questions.takeaway: Use a coordinator-driven refinement loop that evaluates synthesis for gaps and re-delegates targeted work.
